title: Ptolemy chords on a radius-r circle: chord-length formula + law of cosines
description: Generalizes the parent unit-circle Ptolemy machinery (which proves the sine addition formula via chords on radius 1) to a circle of arbitrary radius r ≥ 0, and exposes the two classical chord identities behind Ptolemy's chord tables. chord_length: for z = r·exp(θ_z·i), w = r·exp(θ_w·i), ‖z−w‖ = 2r·|sin((θ_z−θ_w)/2)| — Ptolemy's crd(Δθ) = 2r·sin(Δθ/2). law_of_cosines: ‖z−w‖² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂·cos(θ₁−θ₂) for points at radii r₁, r₂. The two are reconciled on one circle (consistency) by the half-angle identity 1−cos t = 2sin²(t/2), and the r=1 case (chord_length_unit) recovers the parent's distance lemma. Verified in Lean 4, 0 axioms, 0 sorries.

Half-angle / double-angle identity cos t = 1 − 2 sin²(t/2)

overview.historicalContext: Ptolemy's Almagest (c. 150 AD) tabulated chord lengths crd(α) of a circle as a function of the central angle — the ancient world's trigonometric table, where crd(α) on a circle of radius r equals 2r·sin(α/2). Ptolemy's theorem on cyclic quadrilaterals was the engine that let him compute these chords, deriving in effect the sine and cosine addition formulas. The parent gallery entry formalizes that engine on the unit circle to obtain the sine addition formula. This entry restores the explicit radius r and the two identities Ptolemy actually used as a table: the chord-length formula crd(Δθ) = 2r·sin(Δθ/2), and the law of cosines, which gives the third side of a triangle with two sides r₁, r₂ meeting at angle θ₁−θ₂. The law of cosines is itself a generalization of the Pythagorean theorem (the cos = 0 case) and appears in Euclid's Elements (Book II, Props 12–13) in geometric form; the complex-exponential proof here is the modern analytic packaging.
overview.problemStatement: Lift the parent's unit-circle chord computations to a circle of radius r: prove the chord-length formula ‖r·e^{iθz} − r·e^{iθw}‖ = 2r·|sin((θz−θw)/2)| and the law of cosines ‖r₁·e^{iθ₁} − r₂·e^{iθ₂}‖² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂·cos(θ₁−θ₂), and show they are consistent on a single circle.
keyInsights: Scaling separates cleanly: r·e^{iθz} − r·e^{iθw} = r·(e^{iθz} − e^{iθw}), so the radius factors out of the norm as r (for r ≥ 0), reducing everything to the unit-circle chord.
The chord length is governed by the half-angle: 2 − 2cos t = (2 sin(t/2))², which is the squared-chord form of cos t = 1 − 2 sin²(t/2).
The law of cosines is the Cartesian expansion exp(θ·i) = cos θ + i·sin θ followed by the cosine difference formula; the cross term −2r₁r₂cos(θ₁−θ₂) is exactly −2·Re(z·conj w).
On one circle the two formulas must agree, and the bridge is again 1 − cos t = 2 sin²(t/2): law of cosines gives 2r²(1−cos Δθ), chord length gives 4r²sin²(Δθ/2).

Writing exp(θ·i) explicitly via Complex.exp_mul_I (rather than expanding exp_re/exp_im) makes the real/imaginary parts cos θ and sin θ directly, keeping the algebra a one-line linear_combination over the Pythagorean identity.
overview.proofStrategy: Part I proves exp_ofReal_mul_I (Cartesian form) and the unit-circle squared chord normSq_one_sub_exp = 2 − 2cos θ, plus norm_exp_sub_exp factoring exp(b·i) out of a difference of exponentials. Part II proves the half-angle identity two_sub_two_cos via cos_two_mul and the Pythagorean identity. Part III proves chord_length by factoring out r, reducing to the unit chord, squaring, and taking the nonnegative square root (nlinarith). Part IV proves law_of_cosines by rewriting both exponentials in Cartesian form, expanding normSq, applying cos_sub, and closing with a linear_combination over the two Pythagorean identities. Part V derives law_of_cosines_eq_chord_sq and consistency (the formulas agree on one circle) and chord_length_unit (r=1). Part VI gives a worked example: a radius-2 circle, central angle π/3, chord length 2.

sections.title: Overview: lifting Ptolemy's chords to radius r
sections.summary: Docstring: the parent works on the unit circle; this file generalizes to radius r and states the chord-length formula, the law of cosines, their consistency on one circle, and the r=1 specialization.

sections.title: Part I — Cartesian form and the unit-circle squared chord
sections.summary: exp_ofReal_mul_I writes exp(θ·i)=cos θ + i·sin θ. normSq_one_sub_exp proves ‖1 − exp(θ·i)‖² = 2 − 2cos θ. norm_exp_sub_exp factors exp(b·i) out: ‖exp(a·i)−exp(b·i)‖ = ‖1 − exp((a−b)·i)‖.

sections.title: Part II — The half-angle identity
sections.summary: two_sub_two_cos: 2 − 2cos t = (2 sin(t/2))², the squared-chord form of the half-angle identity, via cos_two_mul and sin²+cos²=1.

sections.title: Part III — Chord-length formula on a radius-r circle
sections.summary: chord_length: ‖r·e^{iθz} − r·e^{iθw}‖ = 2r·|sin((θz−θw)/2)| for r ≥ 0 — Ptolemy's crd — by factoring out r, reducing to the unit chord, and taking the nonnegative square root.

sections.title: Part IV — Law of cosines
sections.summary: law_of_cosines: ‖r₁·e^{iθ₁} − r₂·e^{iθ₂}‖² = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂·cos(θ₁−θ₂), via Cartesian expansion, cos_sub, and a linear_combination over the Pythagorean identities.

sections.title: Part V — Consistency and unit-circle specialization
sections.summary: law_of_cosines_eq_chord_sq and consistency show the two formulas agree on a single circle (via the half-angle identity); chord_length_unit recovers the parent's r=1 distance lemma.

sections.title: Part VI — Worked example
sections.summary: A radius-2 circle, central angle π/3 (a regular-hexagon edge): chord length = 2·2·sin(π/6) = 2, checked against chord_length.

crossReferences.description: Parent: proves the sine addition formula from Ptolemy's theorem on the unit circle. This entry lifts its chord computations to radius r and extracts the chord-length and law-of-cosines identities.
The complex-number proof of Ptolemy's theorem itself, whose chord distances this entry computes in closed form.
The law of sines is the companion triangle identity; together with the law of cosines proved here it solves triangles from circle data.

conclusion.summary: On a circle of radius r, the distance between two points at central angles θz, θw is 2r·|sin((θz−θw)/2)| (Ptolemy's chord) and, more generally for radii r₁,r₂, the squared distance is r₁²+r₂²−2r₁r₂cos(θ₁−θ₂) (law of cosines). The two coincide on a single circle via the half-angle identity, and the unit-circle case recovers the parent's distance lemma. All verified with 0 axioms, 0 sorries.
conclusion.implications: These are the two closed-form chord identities Ptolemy needed to build his trigonometric tables, now machine-checked with explicit radius. The law of cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem (the right-angle case) and, with the law of sines, solves arbitrary triangles; the chord formula is the bridge between central angle and chord length used throughout circle geometry.
openQuestions: Use the two-radii squared-distance formula $r_1^2 + r_2^2 - 2r_1 r_2\cos(\theta_1-\theta_2)$ to formalize the full Ptolemy inequality and its equality case (cyclic quadrilaterals) directly in the complex-number setting.

Extend the chord-length identity $2r\,|\sin\tfrac{\theta_z-\theta_w}{2}|$ to spherical and hyperbolic geometry (the non-Euclidean laws of cosines), testing how much of the half-angle machinery survives.
Derive the generalized Ptolemy / Casey theorem (for circles tangent to a common circle, replacing points by tangent circles) from the same half-angle chord identity.

mainTheorems.name: chord_length
mainTheorems.description: Chord-length formula on a circle of radius r: the distance between two points at central angles θz, θw is 2r·|sin((θz−θw)/2)|.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (r θz θw : ℝ), 0 ≤ r → ‖↑r * Complex.exp (↑θz * Complex.I) − ↑r * Complex.exp (↑θw * Complex.I)‖ = 2 * r * |Real.sin ((θz − θw) / 2)|

mainTheorems.name: law_of_cosines
mainTheorems.description: Law of cosines for two points at radii r₁, r₂ and angles θ₁, θ₂: squared distance = r₁² + r₂² − 2r₁r₂cos(θ₁−θ₂).
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (r1 r2 θ1 θ2 : ℝ), ‖↑r1 * Complex.exp (↑θ1 * Complex.I) − ↑r2 * Complex.exp (↑θ2 * Complex.I)‖ ^ 2 = r1 ^ 2 + r2 ^ 2 − 2 * r1 * r2 * Real.cos (θ1 − θ2)

mainTheorems.name: consistency
mainTheorems.description: On a single circle the squared chord length equals the law-of-cosines value, reconciling the two formulas.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (r θz θw : ℝ), 0 ≤ r → ‖↑r * Complex.exp (↑θz * Complex.I) − ↑r * Complex.exp (↑θw * Complex.I)‖ ^ 2 = r ^ 2 + r ^ 2 − 2 * r * r * Real.cos (θz − θw)

mainTheorems.name: chord_length_unit
mainTheorems.description: Unit-circle (r=1) specialization recovering the parent's distance lemma ‖e^{iθz} − e^{iθw}‖ = 2|sin((θz−θw)/2)|.
mainTheorems.leanType: ∀ (θz θw : ℝ), ‖Complex.exp (↑θz * Complex.I) − Complex.exp (↑θw * Complex.I)‖ = 2 * |Real.sin ((θz − θw) / 2)|
